content: Patients who survived their condition often described their recovery as a miracle and shared accounts of the deaths of close family members. All participants viewed clinical cure as a chance for patients to return to their daily routines and regain social and economic productivity. Non-patient stakeholders placed greater importance on achieving clinical cure at six months post-treatment rather than immediately after treatment completion, due to the higher risk of relapse during this period. Most participants believed that the two treatment options did not differ in terms of equity, as both were freely available in public health facilities. However, some expressed concerns about the adverse effects of miltefosine, which rendered pregnant women ineligible for combination therapy. Broader equity issues, such as out-of-pocket expenses in private healthcare settings, were also highlighted for this patient group. Combination therapy was generally considered more acceptable than monotherapy, primarily because of the shorter duration of hospitalization. Longer hospital stays were universally seen as less feasible and less acceptable. Participants emphasized the need for implementation strategies that improve access to treatment, provide counseling, and adopt a holistic approach to care. Research priorities identified included disease epidemiology, diagnostic methods, prevention, disease progression, prognosis, treatment-related issues, immunology, interactions with HIV, and health system integration. Adverse effects of antileishmanial medications were detailed as follows: 1. Miltefosine: Very common: Vomiting, diarrhea. Common: Anorexia, nausea. Uncommon/Rare: Abdominal pain, thrombocytopenia, increased liver enzyme activity, elevated blood urea nitrogen and creatinine, and rare immune reactions like Stevens-Johnson syndrome. 2. Paromomycin: Very common: Pruritus. Common: Nausea, metallic taste, vomiting, headache, lethargy, mild injection-site pain, fever, and reversible audiogram abnormalities. Uncommon/Rare: Injection site swelling, abscess, ototoxicity, conductive deafness, proteinuria, transient increases in liver enzymes, and elevated alkaline phosphatase or bilirubin. 3. Liposomal Amphotericin B: Very common: Pruritus, chills, fever, nausea, vomiting, hypertension, tachycardia, breathlessness, hypoxia, rash, anemia, insomnia, malaise, fatigue, confusion, muscle weakness or cramps. Uncommon/Rare: Chest pain, wheezing, flushing, vasodilation, musculoskeletal pain, stomach pain, headache, bleeding, seizures, infusion site reactions, heart attack, severe swelling, muscle breakdown, and bone/joint pain. 4. Amphotericin B Deoxycholate: Very common: Fever, malaise, weight loss, hypotension, tachypnea, injection site pain, generalized pain, and allergic reactions. Uncommon/Rare: Cardiac arrest, shock, cardiac failure, pulmonary edema, arrhythmias, gastrointestinal symptoms, acute liver failure, anemia, and renal dysfunction. 5. Sodium Stibogluconate: Very common: Flushing, sweating, fever, rash, pain at injection site, abdominal pain, anorexia, malaise, myalgia, arthralgia, headache, and lethargy. Uncommon/Rare: Fatal cardiac arrhythmias, ECG changes, transient coughing, pneumonia, pancreatitis, and blood cell reductions. 6. Meglumine Antimoniate: Very common: Headache, malaise, difficulty breathing, skin rash, and facial edema. Precautions: A protein-rich diet and correction of iron-deficiency anemia or other deficiencies are recommended before systemic administration. These findings underscore the importance of balancing efficacy, safety, and patient-centered considerations in the treatment of leishmaniasis.
